items.plain: We are responsible for who we are, and we can make ourselves whatever we wish. Since what we are now comes from past actions, what we become depends on how we act now.
items.core_idea: Present actions shape who we become.

items.plain: Love, truth and unselfishness are our highest ideal because they hold real power. Working even briefly with no selfish motive makes a person morally strong; holding back is greater power than any outward action.
items.core_idea: Self-restraint is the greatest form of power.

items.plain: You have a right to work, not to its results, so leave the results alone. When you help someone, don't think about how they should treat you; when doing good work, don't worry about the outcome.
items.core_idea: Do the work; let go of the results.

items.plain: The ideal person finds intense activity in deep silence, and the calm of the desert in intense activity. Having mastered himself, he walks busy city streets with a mind as quiet as a cave, working hard all the while.
items.core_idea: Stay inwardly calm while working intensely.

items.plain: We must work and watch what drives us. At first we will find our motives almost always selfish, but with persistence that selfishness slowly melts until we can do truly unselfish work.
items.core_idea: Persistent work slowly melts away selfishness.

items.plain: Once someone starts to hate himself, decline has begun, and the same is true of a nation. Our first duty is not to hate ourselves, because without faith in yourself you can never have faith in God.
items.core_idea: Faith in yourself comes before faith in God.

items.plain: Each person should pursue their own ideal, not someone else's they can never reach. People differ, so mock no ideal and judge no one by another's standard; an apple tree isn't judged as an oak.
items.core_idea: Judge each person by their own ideal.

items.plain: The married householder is as great as the monk, and the street sweeper as great as the king. It is far harder to live in the world and worship God than to give it up for an easy life apart.
items.core_idea: Living in the world and worshipping God is harder.

items.plain: The hardest thing is to work without caring for results, help without expecting thanks, and do good without looking for fame. Anyone can be brave when praised; doing good steadily without anyone's approval is the highest sacrifice.
items.core_idea: Doing good without seeking approval is the highest sacrifice.

items.plain: The Vedas keep repeating one word: fearlessness, fear nothing. Fear is a sign of weakness. A person must go about their duties ignoring the world's sneers and ridicule.
items.core_idea: Fear is weakness; do your duty fearlessly.

items.plain: Giving knowledge is a greater gift than food, clothes or even life itself, because real life is knowledge. Ignorance is death and knowledge is life; a life spent groping in the dark is worth little.
items.core_idea: Knowledge is the greatest gift; ignorance is death.

items.plain: What we repeatedly hear, think and do leaves impressions that drive us without our knowing. Bad impressions push a person toward evil; enough good thoughts and deeds make goodness irresistible, and then good character is established.
items.core_idea: Repeated thoughts and deeds form our character.

items.plain: Work tirelessly, but like a traveller passing through a foreign land, without tying yourself down, because bondage is terrible. This world is not our home, only one of many stages we pass through.
items.core_idea: Work hard but unattached; this world is a passing stage.

items.plain: A man who wants a woman all to himself, jealous of her every move, is a slave who wants her as his slave. That is not love, because it brings pain; real love brings only joy.
items.core_idea: Possessive jealousy is not love; love brings only joy.

items.plain: You expect nothing back from your children. Treat all your work that way: give freely, without thought of return, and your work won't bind you, because attachment comes from expecting returns.
items.core_idea: Give freely, expecting nothing, and attachment disappears.

items.plain: Two forces guide people: power and mercy. Using power is always selfish, since people exploit whatever advantage they have. Mercy is heaven itself; to be good we must be merciful, and even justice should rest on mercy.
items.core_idea: Even justice should rest on mercy.

items.plain: Never boast about what you give the poor or expect their thanks; instead be grateful to them for the chance to be charitable.
items.core_idea: Thank those you help for the chance to give.

items.plain: Only one idea of duty has been accepted by all people everywhere, summed up in a Sanskrit saying: do not harm any being; not harming is virtue and harming is sin.
items.core_idea: Not harming any being is the universal duty.

items.plain: I am not the measure of the universe. I have to adapt myself to the world, not the world to me.
items.core_idea: Adapt yourself to the world, not the reverse.

items.plain: When we start working seriously, life's knocks soon show us where we belong, and no one stays long in a role they don't suit. Lower work doesn't make a lower person; judge people by the spirit in which they work.
items.core_idea: Judge people by how they work, not what work.

items.plain: Duty is rarely sweet; only love makes it run smoothly. Love thrives in freedom, yet being ruled by anger and jealousy is not freedom. Amid life's small irritations, the highest freedom is to hold back.
items.core_idea: Duty is sweet only through love; forbearance is freedom.

items.plain: The only way to rise is to do the duty right in front of you, gaining strength from it, and keep going until you reach the highest state.
items.core_idea: Rise by doing the duty in front of you.

items.plain: When you do any work, don't think of anything beyond it. Do it as worship, the highest worship, and give your whole life to it while you are doing it.
items.core_idea: Do each task wholeheartedly, as worship.

items.plain: Only workers attached to results grumble about their duties; to the unattached, every duty helps kill selfishness and free the soul. The grumbler is never satisfied. Keep doing your duty and you will see the Light.
items.core_idea: Stop grumbling, do your duty, and find the Light.

items.plain: In our busy, material lives our nerves harden and we grow callous with age, ignoring what happens around us. Yet sometimes human nature stirs and we wonder at ordinary things, and that wonder is the first step toward understanding.
items.core_idea: Wondering at ordinary things begins understanding.

items.plain: Call a man a fool and he punches you; speak a few gentle words to a weeping woman and her sorrow lifts and she begins to smile. Words have great power.
items.core_idea: Words have great power to hurt or heal.

items.plain: Life is good or bad according to how we look at it; in itself it is neither. Fire warms us and we praise it, burns us and we blame it, yet it is neutral, and so is the world.
items.core_idea: The mind makes life good or evil.

items.plain: We help someone, expect thanks, and are hurt when none comes. Why expect anything? Be grateful to the one you help and see him as God; without attachment we escape the pain of expectation.
items.core_idea: Help others as worship, expecting no thanks.

items.plain: Don't lose sleep worrying about the world; it will go on without you. Only once you avoid fanaticism will you work well. The calm, level-headed, sympathetic and loving person does good work and so does good to himself.
items.core_idea: The calm, unfanatical worker does the most good.

items.plain: The world will always mix good and evil. Our duty is to sympathise with the weak and love even the wrongdoer. The world is a great moral gym where we all train to grow spiritually stronger.
items.core_idea: The world is a gym for spiritual strength.

items.plain: Whoever sees some evil in good actions, and some good somewhere in evil, has understood the secret of work.
items.core_idea: Every action mixes good and evil.

items.plain: Working for others mainly purifies us, teaching us to forget ourselves, the great lesson of life. True happiness comes from killing selfishness, and only you can make yourself happy. Every kind act shrinks our self-importance, and that is good.
items.core_idea: Serving others purifies us by shrinking the self.

items.plain: Unselfishness is God. Someone can live in a golden palace and be wholly unselfish, and so be in God; another can live in rags with nothing, yet if selfish, be sunk deep in the world.
items.core_idea: Unselfishness, not wealth or poverty, places us in God.

items.plain: Our greatest weakness often passes for our greatest strength: believing others depend on me and that I can do them good. That belief is the root of all attachment, and attachment brings all our pain.
items.core_idea: Thinking others depend on us breeds attachment and pain.

items.plain: Some of your friends may have died this year. Has the world stopped and waited for them to return? No, it goes on.
items.core_idea: The world goes on without any of us.

items.plain: When you give and expect nothing, not even thanks, the person's ingratitude won't hurt you, because you never thought you had a right to anything in return.
items.core_idea: Expect nothing and ingratitude cannot hurt you.

items.plain: Hard as it is to grasp, in time you will learn that nothing in the universe has power over you unless you allow it. Nothing can touch the Self until the Self foolishly gives up its independence.
items.core_idea: Nothing has power over you unless you allow it.

items.plain: To those who haven't mastered their minds, the world seems evil or mixed. Master the mind and it becomes harmonious; some who begin calling it hell end, through self-control, by calling it heaven.
items.core_idea: Master your mind and the world becomes harmonious.

items.plain: No one is ever really taught by another; we each teach ourselves. The explanation of everything lies within you, and an outside teacher only offers a hint that wakes up the teacher inside.
items.core_idea: The real teacher is within you.

items.plain: Are you unselfish? That is the real question. If you are, you will be perfect without reading any religious book or entering any church or temple.
items.core_idea: Unselfishness alone makes you perfect.

items.plain: A river swirls in a whirlpool, then flows on free. Each life is like that: caught in the world, crying 'my family, my name, my fame', then finally breaking out to regain its freedom.
items.core_idea: Every life passes through the world's whirlpool toward freedom.

items.plain: Pain, misery, poverty, wealth and happiness are just passing conditions of this world and are not our real nature, which lies beyond all of them and beyond the senses. Still, we must keep working all the time.
items.core_idea: Our true nature is beyond pleasure and pain.

items.plain: Misery comes from attachment, not from work. If someone else's beautiful painting burns, we barely care; if our own burns, we are heartbroken. The difference is that we identify with one. Thinking 'I and mine' causes all misery.
items.core_idea: 'I and mine' is the source of misery.

items.plain: Someone who gives up home and comforts for the desert can still be deeply attached, even to his body. Non-attachment is in the mind: one person on a throne can be free, another in rags bound.
items.core_idea: Non-attachment is in the mind, not outward circumstances.

items.plain: Look at people enslaved by duty: no time to pray or bathe, working all day and planning tomorrow's work at night. It is a slave's life, ending in dropping dead in harness like a horse.
items.core_idea: Being enslaved by duty is a slave's life.

items.plain: Give whatever you have to give the world, but not out of duty or compulsion. Don't dwell on it. Everything done under compulsion builds attachment.
items.core_idea: Give freely, not from compulsion.

items.plain: Seek no praise or reward for anything. The moment we do good we want credit; give to charity and we want our names in the papers. Such desires bring misery. The greatest people died unknown.
items.core_idea: Seek no credit; the greatest died unknown.

items.plain: The highest people are calm, quiet and unknown. They know the power of thought: even five true thoughts thought alone in a cave will live forever, travel the world, enter human hearts and inspire people to live them out.
items.core_idea: True thoughts, even unspoken, outlive us and spread.

items.plain: Millions of us think we are important in the world, but we all die, and within five minutes the world forgets us.
items.core_idea: The world quickly forgets us all.

items.plain: A lamp lives by constantly burning out; to live, you must die every moment. Life and death are the falling and rising of one wave. The pessimist looks only at the fall, the optimist only at the rise.
items.core_idea: Life and death are one wave rising and falling.

fix.display_text: The lamp is constantly burning out, and that is its life. If you want to have life, you have to die every moment for it. Life and death are only different expressions of the same thing looked at from different standpoints; they are the falling and the rising of the same wave, and the two form one whole. One looks at the “fall” side and becomes a pessimist; another looks at the “rise” side and becomes an optimist.

items.plain: A schoolboy cared for by his parents finds everything wonderful; his needs are simple and he is full of optimism. An old man, after much experience, grows calmer and his warmth cools a great deal.
items.core_idea: Youth is hopeful; experience cools our enthusiasm.

items.plain: The world is a terrible machine of wheels within wheels; once caught in it, we are lost. We think we will rest after finishing one duty, but another is already waiting. We are all dragged along by it.
items.core_idea: The world's demands never let us rest.

items.plain: Do good because doing good is good. Even doing good to reach heaven binds you. Any work done with the slightest selfish motive adds another chain instead of freeing you.
items.core_idea: Do good for its own sake, or it binds you.

items.plain: Every good act done without ulterior motive breaks a link in the chains that bind us. Every good thought sent out without expecting return breaks another, making us purer until we are purest of all.
items.core_idea: Selfless good deeds break our chains.

items.plain: The best worker works with no motive at all, not for money, fame or anything else. Whoever can do that becomes a Buddha, and from him comes the power to work in a way that transforms the world.
items.core_idea: Working without motive transforms the world.

items.plain: Every soul is divine at heart; the goal is to bring out that divinity by mastering nature outside and within, through work, worship, mind control or philosophy, and be free. Doctrines, rituals and temples are secondary.
items.core_idea: Religion is manifesting the divinity within the soul.

items.plain: What right has anyone to claim a soul or God without feeling or seeing them? If they exist we must experience them; otherwise better not to believe. An honest atheist is better than a hypocrite.
items.core_idea: An honest atheist beats a hypocritical believer.

items.plain: Looking deep into his mind, a person can find something eternally pure and perfect. Misery comes from fear and unmet desire; knowing he never dies and is already perfect, he loses both and finds bliss.
items.core_idea: Knowing your undying, perfect nature ends misery.

items.plain: The world will give up its secrets if we knock hard enough, and that force comes from concentration. The mind's power has no limit; the more it focuses on one point, the more power it has.
items.core_idea: Concentration is the secret of the mind's power.

items.plain: Being human is enough. Every person has the right and the power to seek religion, to ask why, and to find the answer for themselves if they take the trouble.
items.core_idea: Everyone has the right to seek truth themselves.

items.plain: When the body is sick the mind gets sick too, and when the body is healthy the mind stays strong. Anger disturbs the mind, and a disturbed mind disturbs the body.
items.core_idea: Body and mind affect each other.

items.plain: Strength is the best guide in life. In religion as in everything, reject whatever makes you weak and have nothing to do with it.
items.core_idea: Reject whatever makes you weak.

items.plain: A young plant needs a fence around it so it isn't damaged; once it becomes a tree, the fence is removed, because it can withstand anything.
items.core_idea: Protect what is young until it grows strong.

items.plain: Practice is essential. You can listen to me for hours every day, but without practice you won't move a step. We only understand these things by experiencing and feeling them ourselves; theories are not enough.
items.core_idea: Only practice and experience bring understanding.

items.plain: No one can stop the body changing even for a moment; it is a flow, like a river whose water is always new yet looks the same. Still, keep it strong and healthy: it is our best instrument.
items.core_idea: The ever-changing body is still our best instrument.

items.plain: Sit upright and silently wish all beings, in every direction, to be happy, peaceful and blissful. The more you do it, the better you feel; making others happy and healthy is the easiest way to be so yourself.
items.core_idea: Wishing others happiness makes us happy.

items.plain: The weak never reach freedom. Throw off all weakness: tell your body and your mind that they are strong, and have boundless faith and hope in yourself.
items.core_idea: Throw off weakness and believe in yourself.

items.plain: Everyone has to start where they are and learn to control what is closest to them. The body is closer than anything in the outside world, and the mind is closest of all.
items.core_idea: Begin by mastering what is nearest: body and mind.

items.plain: Everything in this world is catching, good or bad. If you are tense, strong or sick, those near you tend to become the same.
items.core_idea: Strength and weakness are both contagious.

items.plain: The ocean has mountainous waves, small waves and tiny bubbles, but behind them all is the infinite ocean. Likewise, great or small, every living being is connected to the same infinite store of energy behind all life.
items.core_idea: Every life draws on the same infinite energy.

items.plain: Begin by breathing evenly in and out to bring the body into harmony. Later let a sacred word like 'Om' flow with the breath. Then you will know real rest, deeper than sleep, calming even the most tired nerves.
items.core_idea: Rhythmic breathing with a sacred word brings deep rest.

items.plain: Every child is told 'be good', 'don't steal', 'don't lie', but no one teaches them how to avoid doing these things. Telling is not enough; only teaching them to control their mind really helps.
items.core_idea: Teaching mind control helps more than moral rules.

items.plain: The mind is hard to control, like a restless monkey made drunk, stung by a scorpion and then possessed by a demon. It is restless by nature, drunk with desire, stung by jealousy of others' success, and possessed by pride.
items.core_idea: The mind is a drunk, stung, possessed monkey.

items.plain: Knowledge is power: you can't control the mind until you know what it is doing. Let it run; ugly thoughts may surprise you. But with patient daily practice its wanderings calm, month by month, until it is under full control.
items.core_idea: Watch the mind patiently and it calms down.

items.plain: Be like the pearl oyster of the Indian fable, which catches a special raindrop, closes its shell, dives deep and patiently turns it into a pearl. First hear and understand, then shut out distractions and develop the truth within you.
items.core_idea: Take in truth, then develop it quietly within.

items.plain: Don't waste your energy chasing ideas for their novelty and dropping them for newer ones. Take up one thing and see it through to the end. Only someone who becomes mad about an idea sees light; nibblers achieve nothing.
items.core_idea: Commit to one thing and see it through.

items.plain: Success needs enormous perseverance and will. The persevering soul says it will drink the ocean and crumble mountains at will. Have that kind of energy and will, work hard, and you will reach the goal.
items.core_idea: Tremendous perseverance and will reach the goal.

items.plain: Experience is our only teacher. We can reason all our lives without grasping truth until we experience it. Books don't make a surgeon, and a map only makes you curious to see the country.
items.core_idea: Experience is the only real teacher.

items.plain: While there is desire there is no real happiness; real joy comes from looking on as a calm witness. Animals find happiness in the senses, people in the intellect, gods in contemplation; to the desireless, nature is all beauty.
items.core_idea: Desireless contemplation makes the world beautiful.

items.plain: Non-injury, or Ahimsa, means never causing pain to any living being by thought, word or deed. There is no higher virtue, and no greater happiness than having this harmless attitude toward all creation.
items.core_idea: Non-injury is the highest virtue and happiness.

items.plain: God describes his beloved devotee: one who hates no one, is a friend to all, merciful, selfless, calm in pain and pleasure, content and given to God; unafraid, unmoved by praise or blame, at home everywhere.
items.core_idea: God's beloved devotee is calm, selfless and content.

items.plain: It is certain that every bit of hatred sent out from someone's heart returns to them in full force, and nothing can stop it; likewise every impulse of love comes back.
items.core_idea: Hatred and love both return to the sender.

items.plain: Staying calm is the greatest show of power. Activity is easy, like letting horses bolt; stopping them takes strength. Calm is not dullness: the calm person controls the waves of the mind. Calm is the greater strength.
items.core_idea: Calm is greater strength than activity.

items.plain: When the waves stop and a lake goes still, you can see its bottom. Likewise, when the mind is calm, we see our own true nature and remain ourselves instead of getting mixed up with our thoughts.
items.core_idea: A calm mind reveals our true nature.

items.plain: The highest people are calm, quiet and unknown. They know that even five true thoughts, thought alone in a cave, will live forever, travel the world, and inspire people to live them out.
items.core_idea: Only good habits can reform bad ones.

items.plain: All knowledge is within us, but it must be drawn out by another knowing being; lifeless matter cannot do it. That is why teachers have always been needed.
items.core_idea: Knowledge within us needs a living teacher to awaken.

items.plain: Avoid bad company, because old scars are in you and bad company reopens them. Good company brings out the hidden good impressions in you. Nothing is holier than keeping good company.
items.core_idea: Good company brings out the good in you.

items.plain: Sometimes for days or weeks practice goes well, the mind is calm and you progress fast. Then suddenly progress stops and you feel stuck. Keep going: all progress moves through such ups and downs.
items.core_idea: Persevere; all progress rises and falls.

items.plain: Every reaction of hatred is a loss to the mind, but every one controlled counts in our favour. Restraint is not loss: each time we suppress hatred or anger, good energy is stored and turned into higher powers.
items.core_idea: Restraining anger stores up good energy.

items.plain: Realisation is real religion; everything else, like hearing lectures, reading books or reasoning, only prepares the ground. Agreeing or disagreeing with ideas is not religion.
items.core_idea: Realisation, not belief or study, is religion.

items.plain: The ignorant think the body is the Soul, the learned the mind; both are wrong. Waves in the mind cover the Soul and we see it reflected in them, so we say 'I am angry', 'loving' or 'weak'.
items.core_idea: We mistake the mind's passing waves for the Soul.

items.plain: The senses are the horses, the mind the reins, the intellect the driver, the body the chariot, the Self the rider. If the driver can't control the horses, the chariot crashes; well controlled, it reaches the goal.
items.core_idea: Control the senses through mind and intellect.

items.plain: There are endless books and little time, so the secret of knowledge is to take what is essential and try to live by it.
items.core_idea: Take the essential and live by it.

items.plain: Surrendering the results of work to God means taking neither credit nor blame for yourself, giving both to the Lord, and being at peace.
items.core_idea: Give credit and blame to God and be at peace.

items.plain: When I am angry my mind becomes a huge wave of anger. At first anger and I are separate; then I become it. To truly win, such feelings must be controlled at the root, before we even notice them.
items.core_idea: Control anger at its root, before it takes over.

items.plain: All happiness from the senses eventually brings pain. Every pleasure makes us want more, and human desire has no limit; when desire can't be satisfied, pain follows.
items.core_idea: Sense pleasures breed endless desire and pain.

items.plain: King Yudhishthira said the greatest wonder is that we see people dying every moment yet think we will never die. Amid fools we think ourselves wise; amid fickleness we think our love alone will last.
items.core_idea: We see death everywhere yet think we won't die.

items.plain: Experience of pleasure and pain is the one great teacher, but remember that it is only experience.
items.core_idea: Experience teaches, but it is only experience.

items.plain: It is the people, not the building, that make a church, and we always forget that.
items.core_idea: People, not buildings, make a church.

items.plain: Two opposite ideas come together: that we are bound and that we are free. A wall shows our limits, yet our will feels boundless. We must believe we are free, yet at every moment find we are not.
items.core_idea: We feel both bound and free at once.

items.plain: Hungry for knowledge, we search everywhere, and failing, grow dissatisfied and look elsewhere. All searching is useless until we see that knowledge is within us, that no one else can help us, and that we must help ourselves.
items.core_idea: Knowledge is within; we must help ourselves.

items.plain: To control a big wave of anger, raise an opposite wave: think of love. An angry mother who kisses her baby finds the anger fading as love for the child rises. Love is the opposite of anger.
items.core_idea: Counter anger by raising love.

items.plain: Every hateful thought, even one thought alone in a cave, is stored up and will return to you as misery. Hatred and jealousy come back with compound interest; once set in motion, you must bear them.
items.core_idea: Hateful thoughts return to us with interest.

items.plain: The first sign you are becoming religious is that you are becoming cheerful. Gloominess may be indigestion, but it is not religion.
items.core_idea: Cheerfulness is the first sign of real religion.

items.plain: The more time slips by unnoticed, the more concentrated we are. Absorbed in a book, we lose track of time and are surprised how many hours have passed.
items.core_idea: Losing track of time shows deep concentration.

items.plain: Our misery comes from ignorance, from failing to tell the real from the unreal. We mistake bad for good and the dream for reality. The Soul is the only reality, and we have forgotten it.
items.core_idea: Misery comes from forgetting the Soul, the only reality.

items.plain: We live surrounded by so many miracles, day and night, that we think nothing of them.
items.core_idea: We ignore the miracles all around us.

items.plain: Irrigation water waits in the canal behind gates; open them and it flows in by itself. Likewise all progress and power are already in everyone; perfection is our nature, and once the barrier is removed it rushes in.
items.core_idea: Perfection is already within; remove the barrier.

items.plain: Nothing you do can ever destroy your own glory or true nature, because nothing can touch the soul; a veil is only drawn over it, hiding its perfection.
items.core_idea: Nothing you do can destroy the soul's glory.

items.plain: Nature, like a kind nurse, leads the forgetful soul through every experience and many bodies until it remembers its glory, then returns for others who are lost. Through pleasure and pain, souls flow into perfection.
items.core_idea: Nature guides every soul back to its own perfection.

items.plain: A hawk is miserable if its food is taken away but happy if it gives the food up itself; so whoever gives everything up willingly is happy.
items.core_idea: Giving up willingly brings happiness.

items.plain: Though you may be devoted to many institutions and teachers, take the essence from them all, as a bee takes nectar from many flowers.
items.core_idea: Take the essence from every teacher.

items.plain: Everyone seeks infinite power and infinite pleasure, and most human activity is that struggle. A few soon discover these cannot be reached through the senses, because the senses and body are too limited to express the Infinite.
items.core_idea: The senses are too limited to reach the Infinite.

items.plain: Ethics says 'not I, but you'. It asks us to drop the vain individualism we cling to while seeking the Infinite through the senses. The senses say 'me first'; ethics says 'I must put myself last'.
items.core_idea: Ethics says: put yourself last.

items.plain: Conquering outer nature is grand, but conquering our inner nature is grander. Knowing the laws of the stars and planets is good; knowing the laws of human passions, feelings and will is far better.
items.core_idea: Mastering inner nature is greater than outer.

items.plain: As long as there is death, we must ask whether it ends everything we cling to as real. Facing that abyss, every mind asks: is this real? A lifetime's hopes vanish in a second. Time only sharpens the question.
items.core_idea: Death forces us to ask what is real.

items.plain: We chase the senses to be happy. The successful young man calls life real; old and unfulfilled, he calls it fate, facing a wall he cannot pass. Pleasure, wealth, power, even life itself, all pass away.
items.core_idea: Everything we chase for happiness passes away.

items.plain: Only someone whose life is in the whole universe truly lives; narrowing life to small things brings death and its fear. That fear ends only when you can say: I am in everything, in all lives; I am the universe.
items.core_idea: Seeing yourself in all life ends fear of death.

items.plain: After searching temples, churches, earth and heaven, you come back to your own soul and find that the God you sought and wept for is nearest of all, your own Self. You are already pure and perfect.
items.core_idea: God is your own Self; you are already perfect.

items.plain: Everyone seeks happiness, but most look for it in passing, unreal things. No one has ever found happiness in the senses or sense pleasures. Happiness is found only in the Spirit.
items.core_idea: Happiness is found only in the Spirit.

items.plain: As soon as I think I am just a small body, I want to protect and pamper it at others' expense, and you and I become separate. That idea of separation opens the door to all wrongdoing and all misery.
items.core_idea: Feeling separate from others causes all misery.

items.plain: People today praise doing and look down on thinking, but all work comes from thought. So fill your mind with the highest thoughts and ideals, keep them before you day and night, and great work will follow.
items.core_idea: Great work grows from high thoughts.

items.plain: Why are you crying, friend? For you there is no birth or death, no disease or misery. You are like the endless sky: coloured clouds pass over it and vanish, but the sky stays the same eternal blue.
items.core_idea: You are the unchanging sky; troubles are passing clouds.

items.plain: In the dark, a thief took a tree stump for a policeman, a lover for his sweetheart, a child for a ghost. It was only a stump. We see the world as we are.
items.core_idea: We see the world as we are.

items.plain: Don't talk about the world's wickedness and sin; grieve that you still see wickedness and sin everywhere. If you want to help the world, don't condemn it and make it weaker still.
items.core_idea: Help the world by not condemning it.

items.plain: Let us be brave. Know the Truth and live it. The goal may be far away, but wake up, get up, and don't stop until you reach it.
items.core_idea: Arise, awake, and stop not till the goal.

items.plain: Children are born optimists, and youth hardly believes in death or defeat. Then old age comes, dreams vanish, and the person turns pessimist. Pushed by nature, we swing between extremes without knowing where we go.
items.core_idea: We swing from youthful hope to old despair.

items.plain: Death roams the earth day and night, yet we think we will live forever. Asked what the most wonderful thing on earth was, King Yudhishthira replied that people die around us every day, yet everyone thinks they will never die.
items.core_idea: We see death daily yet think we won't die.

items.plain: Hiding from facts is no remedy. A hare chased by dogs puts its head down and thinks it is safe; when we escape into optimism we do the same, but it solves nothing.
items.core_idea: Blind optimism is hiding, not a remedy.

items.plain: As our capacity for happiness grows, so does our capacity for suffering, perhaps even faster. The more we progress, the more doors open to pain as well as pleasure.
items.core_idea: Greater capacity for joy brings greater capacity for pain.

items.plain: We may imagine a place of only good and no evil, only smiles and no tears, but that is impossible. Whatever can make us smile or happy can also make us cry or miserable.
items.core_idea: Whatever brings joy can also bring sorrow.

items.plain: What I thought good yesterday I no longer think good. Over my life my ideals changed: a fine pair of horses, a certain sweet, then a wife, children and money. Today I laugh at them all as childish nonsense.
items.core_idea: Our ideals keep changing as we grow.

fix.display_text: What I thought to be good yesterday, I do not think to be good now. When I look back upon my life and see what were my ideals at different times, I find this to be so. At one time my ideal was to drive a strong pair of horses; at another time I thought, if I could make a certain kind of sweetmeat, I should be perfectly happy; later I imagined that I should be entirely satisfied if I had a wife and children and plenty of money. Today I laugh at all these ideals as mere childish nonsense.

items.plain: A time comes when the mind wakes from its long, dreary dream, like a child leaving play to go back to its mother. It learns that indulging desire only feeds it, as butter feeds a fire.
items.core_idea: Indulging desire only feeds it, like fire.

items.plain: Fanatics can't really work; they waste three-quarters of their energy. It is the calm, level-headed, practical person who gets work done.
items.core_idea: Calm, practical people work; fanatics waste energy.

items.plain: Someone who says he will work and be happy once the world becomes entirely good is like a man sitting by the Ganges saying he will cross once all the water has flowed into the sea.
items.core_idea: Waiting for a perfect world means never acting.

items.plain: We judge others by our own ideals, but everyone should be judged by theirs. Most quarrels come from judging others' gods, ideals and motives by our own. Someone may do what I would do for an entirely different reason.
items.core_idea: Judge others by their ideals, not yours.

items.plain: One impulse in the mind says 'do', and behind it another voice says 'don't'. Our ideas constantly push outward through the senses, but behind them a tiny, faint voice says 'don't go outside'.
items.core_idea: A quiet inner voice pulls us back from the senses.

items.plain: We cannot live together without putting up with each other and holding ourselves back. All society rests on restraint, and anyone who hasn't learned to bear and forbear lives a very miserable life.
items.core_idea: Living together requires bearing and forbearing.

items.plain: We have strong cravings we can't satisfy; every step forward brings a blow, like Tantalus. Our high ideals can't find expression and the crowd crushes us. Yet giving up ideals to just survive makes us brutish. Neither way brings happiness.
items.core_idea: Neither chasing nor abandoning ideals brings happiness.

items.plain: What you don't set free will never grow. Thinking you can guide others' growth while keeping all freedom for yourself is a dangerous lie that has held back millions. Liberty is the only condition of growth.
items.core_idea: Freedom is the only condition of growth.

items.plain: Denouncing an evil won't remove it. Go to the root: find the cause and remove it, and the effect will go too.
items.core_idea: Remove the cause, not just denounce the evil.

items.plain: Whoever sees the One running through this world of many things, finds the One Infinite Life in this world of death, and the One Light in this world of ignorance, has eternal peace, and no one else.
items.core_idea: Eternal peace belongs to those who see the One.

items.plain: We arrive crying and fight our way through life's endless ocean as best we can, with ages behind us and vast stretches ahead, until death takes us off the field, and we don't know whether we won or lost.
items.core_idea: We struggle through life not knowing if we win.

items.plain: We seek happiness where it can't be found. Though told for ages it is futile, we learn only by experience, and not even then. Like moths into a flame we keep hurling ourselves at sense pleasures until we die cheated.
items.core_idea: Like moths, we keep chasing pleasures that burn us.

items.plain: You can't hide rotting flesh under roses for long; the roses fade and it is worse than before. So with our lives: we may cover festering sores with gold cloth, but one day it is removed.
items.core_idea: You cannot hide decay for long.

items.plain: Today's beautiful, hopeful young person is tomorrow's old veteran. Hopes, joys and pleasures will die like blossoms in tomorrow's frost.
items.core_idea: Youth and its joys fade like blossoms.

items.plain: One person stumbles more than another; we call the one who stumbles more bad and the one who stumbles less good. Good and bad are not different things but the same, differing only in degree.
items.core_idea: Good and bad differ in degree, not kind.

items.plain: A small fish fleeing enemies in the water escaped by growing wings and becoming a bird. It didn't change the water or the air; it changed itself. Change always happens within.
items.core_idea: Real change comes from within.

items.plain: Life's great inspirations come through the heart. Better a little heart and no brain than all brain and no heart, which withers. Yet heart alone falls into pitfalls; we need heart and head together.
items.core_idea: We need heart and head together.

items.plain: The Lord is equally present in life and death, in happiness and misery. The whole world is full of the Lord. Open your eyes and see Him.
items.core_idea: The Lord is present everywhere; open your eyes.

items.plain: What makes us miserable? Desire causes all our suffering. You want something, don't get it, and you are distressed. Without desire there is no suffering.
items.core_idea: Desire is the cause of all suffering.

items.plain: We've done many things we wish we hadn't, yet they taught us much. I'm glad of my good deeds and my many mistakes, since each was a lesson. I am the result of all I have done and thought.
items.core_idea: Our mistakes are lessons; we are their sum.

items.plain: Jesus said the kingdom of heaven is within you, and so do the Vedanta and every great teacher. In ignorance we roamed the world weeping for the truth, while it lived all along in our own hearts.
items.core_idea: The truth we seek is within our hearts.

items.plain: Who enjoys a painting, the seller or the viewer? The seller is busy counting his profit and watching the bids. The one who enjoys it is the person who came with no intention of buying or selling and simply looks.
items.core_idea: Only those who want nothing truly enjoy.

items.plain: Plunging into foolish luxury without knowing the truth misses the goal. So does cursing the world, fleeing to a forest and starving body and feeling until you are harsh and dried up. Both extremes lose the way.
items.core_idea: Both indulgence and harsh self-denial miss the goal.

items.plain: We are dying of thirst beside the mightiest river and of hunger beside heaps of food. The universe is full of bliss, yet we are in it all the time and keep mistaking it.
items.core_idea: Bliss surrounds us, yet we fail to see it.

items.plain: It's easy to talk about seeing God in everyone. But when a strong man shoves me onto the pavement, I jump up with clenched fists, the thought gone. Instead of meeting God, I see the devil.
items.core_idea: Seeing God in everyone vanishes at the first shove.

items.plain: In Aesop's fable, a stag boasts of his strength, then flees when dogs bark; his confidence vanishes at the sound. We are the same: bold in our resolutions, but we run when trial and temptation bark.
items.core_idea: Our confidence vanishes when trials come.

fix.display_text: You all remember how in Æsop’s Fables a fine stag is looking at his form reflected in a lake and is saying to his young one, “How powerful I am, look at my splendid head, look at my limbs, how strong and muscular they are; and how swiftly I can run.” In the meantime he hears the barking of dogs in the distance, and immediately takes to his heels, and after he has run several miles, he comes back panting. The young one says, “You just told me how strong you were, how was it that when the dog barked, you ran away?” “Yes, my son; but when the dogs bark all my confidence vanishes.” Such is the case with us. We think highly of humanity, we feel ourselves strong and valiant, we make grand resolves; but when the “dogs” of trial and temptation bark, we are like the stag in the fable.

items.plain: Most people grope through life with no ideal at all. If someone with an ideal makes a thousand mistakes, someone without one makes fifty thousand. So it is better to have an ideal.
items.core_idea: Better to have an ideal, even with mistakes.

items.plain: Don't mind failures; they are natural, the beauty and poetry of life, which would be worthless without struggle. Only a cow never lies. Hold to your ideal, and if you fail a thousand times, try once more.
items.core_idea: Fail a thousand times, then try once more.
